title: Made a little planet where LLM NPCs remember you and run their own economy — next they'll build their own towns. What would you add?
author: Novel-Cantaloupe8236
selftext:
Dev build I've been messing with: a tiny round planet you roam as a courier.

The catch — the towns are a live sim, not scenery:

* NPCs work, trade and earn on their own
* talk to any of them via an LLM and they actually remember you
* friendships, weather, crafting, gifting all feed back in

Next up: NPCs \*and\* players build and expand their own buildings, so towns visibly change over time.

What "spice" would you add to make a self-evolving town worth hanging around in?

※Since the in-game time was late at night during the video, no NPCs were visible. Only the appearance of the sky is shown in fast-forward.

comments.author: EnumeratedArray
comments.body:
It's a cool concept, but where's the fun?

If the fun is seeing the town evolve? It looks too big to consume and see changes over time.

If it's LLM NPCs, what makes interacting with them fun, when I could just talk to any LLM online?

replies.author: Novel-Cantaloupe8236
replies.body:
good question, honestly, and a fair one.

one of the core ideas is that the town changes based on what you do. buildings get rebuilt, and eventually maybe whole new towns form (that part's still a pipe dream, i'll admit). but you're right that if you can't actually notice the change, it's not fun. so here's what i'm chewing on: if you could own a house in a town, maybe you'd get attached to it and actually care how it grows?

and on the NPCs, honestly, just talking to an LLM isn't fun by itself, i'm with you. I want to go past basic chatting and have their behavior shift based on how the interactions actually play out.

replies.author: EnumeratedArray
replies.body:
I get the vision, but the world changing based on what you do only works if there's stuff to do.

From what it looks like so far, there's nothing to do.

replies.author: Novel-Cantaloupe8236
replies.body:
that makes sense. there is a courier loop with deliveries, errands and some gather/craft, but honestly it's thin right now, not enough to make you want to act (i haven't really been able to show any of it in the video either 😅).

so you're right, the real gap is a compelling reason to do anything in the first place. still figuring that part out. if you've got a cool idea for what would pull a player in, i'd love to hear it.

honestly, fully LLM-based NPCs are the dream, and where i want to end up too. it's mainly rule-based right now so it's cheap and doesn't hallucinate, but the goal isn't to stay all-rules. it's to keep rules as the floor and gradually let the LLM decide more of the behavior, pushing that ratio up where it's worth the cost.

would be cool to see the town evolve and things play out with or without your involvement I like the idea just sounds complicated and expensive

replies.author: Novel-Cantaloupe8236
replies.body:
honestly, right now it's mostly the rule-based side. the NPCs run hand-authored daily routines off the in-game clock, and there's no LLM in the behavior itself yet.

what i'm building toward is a hybrid: an interface where an LLM can nudge and vary that base behavior, so certain NPCs break their routine in ways the rules alone wouldn't.

and your cost worry is spot on. so to start, i want to try it on just the main NPCs rather than all of them, and see how much it changes the feel. the small-planet setup also caps how many NPCs there are, which keeps it affordable.

comments.author: Redrat2k6
comments.body:
This is super cool. All the AI haters are going to be left in the dust one day with only themselves to blame. 

I had a cool idea you could add. It's kinda big though. What if your game tracked things with tags and properties (NPCs, items, locations, factions, reputation, relationships, quest status, etc.) as context for the LLM? When the player begins a conversation, the game engine would send only the relevant tagged information to the LLM. The LLM would generate dialogue and suggest interactions or quests based on the tags, then the game engine would validate all the tags (make sure they are context and setting appropriate) and generate dialogue or even quests for the character.

For example a backpack could have a "storage**"** tag. Any item placed inside automatically gains a "hidden" tag. During dialogue, NPCs would never mention items with the "hidden" tag unless they had a skill or perception check that successfully detected the item. If they did notice the item, they could also react to any other tags its other tags like "Illegal" "Banana" "Drug".  That could naturally create mechanics like smuggling, inspections, bribery, or suspicion without requiring you to write dialogue for every possible situation.

replies.author: Novel-Cantaloupe8236
replies.body:
genuinely nice idea, and close to where i want to head. tags solve the two things that scare me about the LLM, cost and hallucination. you send only the relevant tags (small, cheap context), and the engine validates whatever the LLM proposes against them, so the world stays the source of truth, not the model. LLM suggests, engine decides.

and the hidden/illegal/perception example turning into smuggling and bribery with no hand-written lines is exactly the emergent behavior i'm chasing. big one, so not overnight, but it's the right shape. thanks for laying it out.
